sentences.text: Borealopelta was an extinct herbivorous ankylosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
This animal measured 5.5 meters long and weighed 1.3 metric tons, or approximately 1,300 kilograms.
Unlike many relatives, it had a straight tail instead of a club and bore a pair of long shoulder spines shaped like bull horns.
The fossil preserves armor osteoderms in their living positions, including numerous closely spaced rows of small plates covering the top and sides of its wide body.
The generic name Borealopelta derives from the Latin "borealis" meaning "north" and Greek "pelta" meaning "shield", referencing the northern locality and preserved osteoderms.
The fossil preserved armor in life position, keratin sheaths, skin, and stomach contents, making it one of the most complete specimens of its size ever found.
Melanosomes found in the fossil indicate the animal had a reddish-pink or reddish-brown shaded skin tone used for camouflage.
It possessed a flexible keratin layer up to 16 cm thick that could withstand forces over 125,000 joules per square meter.
The species B. markmitchelli was named in 2017 by Caleb Brown and colleagues based on a specimen known as the Suncor nodosaur.
The holotype was uncovered on March 21, 2011, at the Millennium Mine, 30 km north of Fort McMurray, Alberta.
The specimen was discovered by a miner named Shawn Funk.
The specific name B. markmitchelli honors Mark Mitchell for his over 7,000 hours of patient and specialized preparation of the holotype.
Stomach contents indicate that ferns were a major part of Borealopelta's diet, and charcoal suggests it fed in an area recovering from a recent wildfire.
Researchers inferred the animal died only a few hours after ingesting ferns in early or mid-summer.
The body of Borealopelta must have been washed into the sea by waves, perhaps during a flood, where a siderite concretion began forming around the carcass shortly after it reached the sea floor.
Borealopelta is classified within the family Nodosauridae.
It is also classified within the class Ornithischia.
Phylogenetic analysis placed Borealopelta in a clade with other nodosaurids, including Pawpawsaurus campbelli, Europelta carbonensis, and Hungarosaurus tormai as a sister taxon.

Borealopelta lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, about 110–112 million years ago, while other sources place the time range in the Aptian stage from 121.4 to 113.2 million years ago.

At the time, the region was covered by the Western Interior Seaway, an inland sea, and the Suncor specimen was preserved in marine sandstones and shales of the Wabiskaw Member of the Clearwater Formation.
A siderite concretion formed around the carcass, preventing scavenging and preserving the body intact.
